extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy; philosophers and educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and analysis of the nature and limits of human reason (epistemology and practical reason), and an account/evaluation of Stoic ethics and its aims (happiness, ataraxia, virtue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical evidence is a priori perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidence of mathematics rests essentially not upon demonstration, but upon immediate perception which is a priori and therefore independent of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations are often foreign and add nothing we were not already convinced of; mathematical certainty comes from the immediate, unified form of knowledge allowing one to proceed from reason to consequent (cause → effect). Example: equality of sides known from equality of angles. Anti-pattern: valuing only stilted logical demonstration while ignoring immediate a priori insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical knowledge is inductive and not unconditionally certain
rubrics_metrics.description: All knowledge through sense-perception and the greater part of experience proceeds from the consequent to the reason (induction) and therefore is not infallible or unconditionally certain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because we cannot have all cases before us, induction approaches but does not attain necessity; rare exceptions (e.g., situs inversus: heart on right side) show residual possibility of error. Use repeated confirmation to increase practical certainty but acknowledge residual uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori sciences permit reasoning from cause to effect (necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a priori sciences (mathematics, pure natural science, logic) the formal element is given as a whole allowing one to proceed from the cause to the effect, and thus these sciences have necessity unavailable to empirical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their advantage lies in starting from reasons rather than consequents. This is why mathematics/logic can be discovered 'all at once' whereas natural science requires accumulated experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-arranged experiments allow cause→effect certainty but presuppose hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Only purposely arranged experiments make knowledge proceed from the cause to the effect and thus follow the method that affords certainty; however these experiments are themselves undertaken because of hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental certainty is possible locally but is grounded on prior hypotheses; natural science progresses by replacing false hypotheses with better ones through accumulated experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error arises from inferring the reason from the consequent (overgeneralized induction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every error is an inference from the consequent to the reason which is valid only if the consequent could have no other reason; otherwise the inference rests on an unjustified universal ('always') where 'sometimes' or 'generally' would be correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common causes of this error: haste, insufficient knowledge of possibilities, falsely generalized major premises. Examples: mistaking a painting for an alto-relief; assuming servant must have key when safe empty; misconstruing prism spectrum leading to false theory. Remedy: avoid unwarranted universal claims and seek full induction where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusion and error are analogous (perception vs reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: Illusion (deception of the senses) and error (deception of the reason) are analogous: both are inferences from effect to cause; illusion occurs in perception, error in thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace mistakes to wrong inferences from effects to causes. Except for certain simple counting mistakes, errors usually result from faulty generalization rather than mere computational slip.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific explanation ultimately ends at a qualitas occulta
rubrics_metrics.description: Every explanation that does not lead to a relation of which no 'why' can further be demanded stops at an accepted 'qualitas occulta' (an original force or inner nature) which remains inexplicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural science explains relations of phenomena but must ultimately presuppose inexplicable elements (e.g., matter, life, species differences). Accept that some aspects (thing-in-itself) lie beyond the principle of sufficient reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of sufficient reason limits explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanation is the establishment of relations according to the applicable form of the principle of sufficient reason; this principle itself and what lies outside it (the thing-in-itself) are ultimately inexplicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different sciences employ different forms of the principle; philosophy uniquely questions the principle itself rather than presupposing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy begins where science ends; presupposes nothing
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy treats everything as equally external and problematic, presupposing nothing known; it cannot rest upon demonstrations that assume prior principles because for philosophy everything is in need of proof or examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy's method is distinct from science: instead of accepting a foundation it interrogates the foundations themselves (including the principle of sufficient reason).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for philosophy = knowing the one in the many (abstraction & unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy requires the ability to abstract and to present the manifold of the world under a few universal concepts — to know the one in the many and the many in the one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy must form a systematic 'recapitulation' or reflection of the world in abstract concepts, separating and uniting particulars into universals so that the whole is comprehended and mutual deducibility of judgments becomes possible (though they must all be present to ground the first judgment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reason is distinct from moral worth (critique of Kant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical reason — reason as a guide of action — is not the immediate source of virtue or moral worth as Kant claimed; rational action and virtuous action are distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reason can equally support good or evil ends and is neutral regarding moral worth; ethical merit requires more than merely acting rationally (see author's Appendix/Fundamental Problems of Ethics for detailed refutation of Kant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic ethics aim at happiness via inner peace (ataraxia); virtue as means
rubrics_metrics.description: The Stoical philosophy develops practical reason to the highest degree: its aim is happiness through peace of mind (ataraxia), and virtue appears as the means to that end rather than as an end in itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stoicism values rational life and tranquility; virtue is instrumental to tranquillity. This differs from ethical systems that place virtue as the immediate end (e.g., Plato, Christianity, Kant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoic practice: distinguish what depends on us versus what does not
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid pain and anxiety one should distinguish carefully what depends upon us (the will) and what does not, and avoid counting upon what is not in our control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus only on maxims (which are in our power) rather than consequences or external circumstances. By aligning desires with what is possible and recognizing transience, one reduces suffering. Epictetus and Chrysippus cited in support; examples: reducing expectations, proportioning desires to what is attainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical living requires harmony with oneself and nature (Stoic variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Zeno's principle to 'live in harmony with oneself' and the later addition to 'live in harmony with nature' (interpreted either as whole nature or specifically human nature) grounds Stoic ethics; determining one's conduct rationally supplies material content to the formal maxim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be consistent, one must set maxims rationally and persist with them regardless of changing impressions; different Stoic thinkers (Zeno, Kleanthes, Chrysippus) nuance 'nature' differently (general nature vs human nature).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason provides a double life (abstract reflection + concrete action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human reason creates a second, abstract life (a 'reduced plan' or chart of one's life) in which one can reflect and act with deliberation beyond immediate perception, enabling actions that brutes cannot perform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This double life yields calm deliberation enabling actions like facing death or danger with composure; but the value of abstract knowledge lies only in its relation to perceived reality, not as an end in itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason alone cannot fully abolish suffering; contradiction in seeking a suffering-free life
rubrics_metrics.description: Although reason can greatly lessen suffering and produce a kind of philosophical happiness, there is an absolute contradiction in expecting to live without suffering; total freedom from suffering via reason alone is unattainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text signals a fuller exposition to follow; treat claims of complete liberation from life's pain via pure rationality with skepticism and expect further argumentation.
